query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles, the onset and progression of phase transition in the premelting/melting regime is driven by the preferential surface segregation and enhanced diffusivity of Cu, whose lower melting point locally reduces the free-energy barrier. This Cu‐rich quasi-liquid surface layer initiates a premelting stage that propagates inward, lowering the effective transition temperature relative to bulk estimates and displaying a size‐dependent effect.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid, equiatomic FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles (∼5 nm in diameter) with a homogeneous element distribution in the as‐synthesized state.
generation.intervention: Heat samples under controlled inert atmosphere (e.g., Ar) at specified ramp rates (e.g., 5 K/min) to temperatures approaching and exceeding the expected premelting range, while running a controlled comparison alloy in which Cu is replaced by a higher-melting element (or omitted) to suppress the surface segregation effect.
generation.conditions: Inert atmosphere, controlled heating rate (5 K/min), nanoparticle size distribution centered around 5 nm, and identical sample preparation to limit extrinsic oxidation or support interactions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a Cu-enriched surface layer (quasi-liquid shell) mediating atomic rearrangement due to the high surface-to-volume ratio of nanoparticles.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures near the melting regime, Cu atoms—due to their lower melting point—diffuse to the nanoparticle surface more readily than the other constituent atoms, thereby locally lowering the melting point at the surface. This initiates a premelting (or surface melting) phenomenon that destabilizes the interatomic bonds and triggers progressive melting from the surface inward. The effect is amplified in smaller particles given their high surface area, leading to an overall transition occurring at temperatures lower than predicted by bulk mixing rules.
generation.predicted_outcome: DSC/DTA measurements will reveal an additional endothermic event at a temperature lower than the bulk melting point, corresponding to the onset of premelting. High-resolution elemental mapping (e.g., EDS or STEM-EELS) after short dwell times at this temperature will show Cu enrichment at the nanoparticle surfaces. In comparison, the control alloy lacking Cu will not exhibit this early endothermic signature or surface segregation, maintaining a more uniform thermal transition.
generation.baseline: The thermal response (melting onset temperature and progression) and elemental distribution in the initially homogeneous FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles measured by DSC and microscopy prior to heating.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is valid under conditions where nanoparticles are free-standing, inert atmosphere precludes oxidation, and heating rates are slow enough (≈5 K/min) to allow for measurable atomic diffusion but fast enough to retain nanoscale effects. It may not hold under conditions of extreme pressure or when particle sizes are significantly larger (e.g., >50 nm) where bulk behavior dominates.
generation.uncertainty: While prior nanoparticle synthesis studies (e.g., laser-induced rapid heating in PMC11427457 and thermal analysis of HEAs in PMC7956699) indicate that surface effects and kinetic factors govern phase transitions, direct evidence of element-specific surface segregation in FeNiCrCoCu under controlled premelting conditions is not currently established. The new aspect of this proposal is specifically transferring the concept of a Cu-driven surface premelting mechanism to FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles, supported by the known effects of size-dependent surface energy (as seen in disorder-to-order transitions in similar systems, e.g., PMC8797181) and the reported role of compositional heterogeneity on thermal stability (PMC11265590).

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles: one set of FeNiCrCoCu HEA nanoparticles and one control set where Cu is replaced by a refractory element (e.g., FeNiCrCoAl). Heat both samples under identical inert conditions using DSC with concurrent in situ high-resolution TEM/EDS characterization. Monitor thermal events and element-specific surface composition during heating.
measurements: DSC/DTA curves to identify onset temperatures of endothermic events.
In situ or ex situ elemental mapping (EDS or STEM-EELS) of heated particles to assess Cu surface enrichment.
Particle size analysis pre- and post-heating.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles do not show an extra endothermic event at a temperature lower than the bulk melting point, or if high-resolution mapping fails to reveal significant Cu enrichment at the particle surfaces compared to the control, then the hypothesis that Cu-driven surface segregation drives the premelting phase transition will be falsified.

In this paper, thermal analysis of the CoCrFeMo0.85Ni HEA powder was carried out via differential thermal analysis (DTA) and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to assess the thermodynamic properties of HEA, including the solidus, liquidus and phase transition temperatures. With detailed characterization of microstructures in the DTA sample, the critical temperatures determined in thermal analysis can be correlated with microstructural features to examine phase formation and formation of precursor states from compositional modulations in HEA. This will provide fundamental understanding on intermetallic strengthening mechanism and phase stability for processing of HEAs.

We attribute the size effect on the disorder-to-order transition to the difference in surface energy. MPEIs have a lower surface energy than HEAs, as MPEIs forms stronger atom-atom interactions (). Because of the large relative surface area of small nanoparticles, we hypothesize that the difference in the surface energy between MPEI and HEA small nanoparticles (~5 nm) play a key role in driving the disorder-to-order transition. It is also possible that the larger particles (e.g., 10 to 20 nm) need to overcome a higher energy barrier to complete the disorder-to-order transition (). For the particles substantially larger than 5 nm (e.g., 150 nm), such a large energy barrier could hinder the formation of fully ordered MPEIs. The disorder-to-order transition is thermodynamically favored to form phase-stable MPEI nanoparticles. We verified the lower enthalpy of the MPEI nanoparticles with a size of 4 to 5 nm by conducting high-temperature oxide melt drop solution calorimetry () on the quinary and octonary MPEIs and their corresponding disordered HEA starting materials.
